error_modes.label: Altitude control during the VFR departure / SID climb

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude set without reference to the departure altitude restriction, did not arrest the climb at the assigned altitude and did not level off at the published segment limit. The excursion passed 300 feet from the assigned altitude and continued to increase. The IP intervened to establish level flight before the next segment of the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to delayed recognition of the level-off point, did not lead the capture of the assigned departure altitude and allowed the deviation to reach 300 feet, the outer limit of the standard. The correction was applied only after the IP verbally prompted an altitude check. Level flight was regained late, after the departure turn had already been started.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unadjusted through the departure turn, did not hold the assigned altitude and drifted 200 feet from it. SP detected the trend on the altimeter and returned the aircraft inside 150 feet without any prompt. The remaining segments of the departure were flown at the assigned altitudes.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned departure altitudes within 150 feet throughout the VFR departure and the SID. Each level-off was led early enough that no overshoot developed at any altitude restriction. Altitude was cross-checked at every segment change of the departure.
texts.4: SP held every assigned altitude of the departure with deviations that remained negligible on the altimeter. Each level-off was anticipated and flown with no measurable overshoot at any restriction. Altitude control was preserved through the climbing turns and the configuration changes without degradation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the departure altitudes inside the standard, but the deviations repeatedly reached the upper part of the acceptable band during the climbing turns. The corrections were technically correct yet consistently reactive rather than anticipated. SP is expected to lead the level-offs earlier so that altitude keeping does not depend on late corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure climb with IP calling the level-off lead point and confirming the assigned altitude alongside SP, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown holding a specific altitude through climbing turns rather than a general climb. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to judge more of the level-off lead point independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the departure altitude to about 300 feet from the assigned value, at the edge of the standard, due to the level-off lead point being judged only as the assigned altitude was reached rather than before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to judge the lead point before the assigned altitude is reached, not as it arrives.
texts_at.2: SP held the departure altitude to about 210 feet from the assigned value, due to the power setting being adjusted a beat after the climbing turn rather than through it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to adjust power through the climbing turn rather than a beat after it.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure altitude to about 150 feet from the assigned value, due to the altitude cross-check at the segment change coming a fraction after the turn rather than through it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to cross-check altitude through the turn, not a fraction after it.

texts_above.1: SP held the departure altitude to about 280 feet from the assigned value, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the assigned departure altitudes to about 200 feet throughout the climb, leading each level-off early enough that no overshoot developed at any restriction. Cross-checking altitude through the turn itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude-lead discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned departure altitudes to about 130 feet throughout the VFR departure and the SID, cross-checking altitude at every segment change without the workload of the departure disturbing it. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead a moment earlier on the steepest climb segment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude-lead discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held every assigned altitude of the departure with deviations that remained negligible on the altimeter, each level-off anticipated and flown with no measurable overshoot with altitude control preserved through the climbing turns and configuration changes. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude-lead discipline.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control on the departure climb schedule

texts.0: SP, due to a power lever position not matched to the briefed climb schedule, did not maintain the departure climb airspeed and allowed the deviation to exceed 20 knots. The airspeed continued to diverge while SP worked the navigation display. The IP took over the power setting to re-establish the briefed departure speed.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the course indication during the initial climb, did not monitor the airspeed and let it reach 20 knots from the briefed departure speed, at the limit of the standard. The trend was reversed only after repeated verbal reminders from the IP. The briefed speed was re-established late in the departure segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction at the level-off, did not hold the briefed departure speed and accelerated 15 knots above it. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the speed inside 10 knots without prompting. Airspeed control remained stable for the rest of the departure.
texts.3: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID climb at the briefed airspeed within 10 knots. Power changes at the level-offs and at the configuration changes were made early enough to prevent any speed excursion. Airspeed was included in the cross-check at every segment of the departure.
texts.4: SP held the briefed departure airspeed with deviations that were negligible throughout the profile. Power was set precisely at each transition, so no speed trend was ever allowed to develop. Airspeed accuracy was maintained while SP simultaneously managed the navigation and the radio.
texts.marginal: SP kept the departure airspeed within the standard, but the excursions repeatedly approached the outer part of the tolerance after each power change. Speed was recovered correctly, yet only after the deviation had become visible on the indicator. SP is expected to set power to the known climb values so that speed is held rather than chased.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure climb with IP calling the power settings needed to hold the briefed airspeed schedule, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown to a specific climb schedule rather than a general climb power. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to set more of the power settings independently to the climb schedule on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the departure airspeed to about 20 knots from the briefed value, at the edge of the standard, due to the power setting being read off the indicator trend rather than set to a known climb value. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set power to a known climb value rather than reading it off the trend.
texts_at.2: SP held the departure airspeed to about 15 knots from the briefed value, due to the power reduction at level-off coming a beat after the course indication was checked rather than with it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reduce power with the course check, not a beat after it.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure airspeed to about 10 knots from the briefed value, due to the power change at one configuration change trailing the transition by a fraction. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the power change in the same instant as the configuration change.

texts_above.1: SP held the departure airspeed to about 18 knots from the briefed value, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID climb at the briefed airspeed to about 15 knots, making power changes early enough at the level-offs and configuration changes to prevent any speed excursion. Making the power change in the same instant as the configuration change, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-setting discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID climb at the briefed airspeed to about 8 knots, with airspeed included in the cross-check at every segment of the departure. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the busiest segment change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-setting discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed departure airspeed with deviations that were negligible throughout the profile, power set precisely at each transition so no speed trend was ever allowed to develop while the navigation and the radio were worked simultaneously. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-setting discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a departure heading taken from the wrong segment of the plan, did not fly the assigned departure track and allowed the heading error to grow beyond 10 degrees. The aircraft diverged from the published ground track with no correction applied. The IP intervened to re-establish the aircraft on the departure course.
texts.1: SP, due to a rollout flown without reference to the target heading, did not stop the turn on the assigned departure heading and settled 10 degrees off it, at the limit of the standard. The correction was made only after the IP identified the error verbally. The assigned track was regained after a delay.
texts.2: SP, due to an uncompensated crosswind on the initial departure leg, did not hold the assigned heading and drifted 8 degrees from it. SP recognized the drift against the heading indicator and re-established the assigned heading within 5 degrees without prompting. The remaining legs of the departure were flown on the planned track.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned departure headings within 5 degrees throughout the VFR departure and the SID. Turns were rolled out on the target heading without overshoot. Drift correction was applied so that the published ground track was preserved.
texts.4: SP flew every assigned departure heading with negligible deviation. Rollouts were anticipated so that no secondary correction was required after any turn. The ground track matched the published departure throughout, including on the crosswind legs.
texts.marginal: SP held the departure headings inside the standard, but each rollout required a secondary correction before the target heading was captured. The track was maintained, yet with a repeated pattern of small overshoots. SP is expected to lead the rollout so that the assigned heading is captured on the first attempt.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure heading with IP calling the rollout point for each turn and confirming the drift correction, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown holding an assigned heading through the turns. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to judge more of the rollout points independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the departure heading to about 10 degrees from the assigned value, at the edge of the standard, due to the rollout lead point being judged only as the turn neared completion rather than earlier in it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to judge the rollout lead point earlier in the turn, not as it nears completion.
texts_at.2: SP held the departure heading to about 7 degrees from the assigned value, due to the crosswind correction on the initial leg being recognized a beat after roll-out rather than anticipated before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to anticipate the crosswind correction before roll-out, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure heading to about 5 degrees from the assigned value, due to the drift correction being applied a fraction after roll-out rather than in the same motion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the drift correction in the same motion as the rollout.

texts_above.1: SP held the departure heading to about 9 degrees from the assigned value, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the assigned departure headings to about 7 degrees throughout the departure, rolling out of each turn on the target heading with drift correction applied so the published ground track was preserved. Applying the drift correction in the same motion as the rollout, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid rollout-lead discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned departure headings to about 4 degrees throughout the VFR departure and the SID, with turns rolled out on the target heading without overshoot. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead through the tightest turn of the departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed rollout-lead discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew every assigned departure heading with negligible deviation, rollouts anticipated so no secondary correction was required after any turn with the ground track matching the published departure throughout, including on the crosswind legs. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding rollout-lead discipline.

error_modes.label: Completion of required procedures before Zero Point

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the departure phase, did not complete the required procedures before Zero Point and arrived over it with the checks and the navigation setup unfinished. The aircraft was not established at the planned parameters at the point where the route timing had to start. The IP intervened to close the outstanding items and to establish the aircraft on the first leg.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit work inside the departure turn, did not finish the required procedures before Zero Point and completed them only after crossing it. The items were actioned only after the IP called for them. The first leg was begun with the departure setup still in progress and the timing reference taken late.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the pre-Zero Point sequence, did not have all required procedures complete on first reaching the point, but recognized the shortfall and closed them within seconds of it. No item was omitted and the timing was started correctly. The first leg was then flown as planned without further disruption.
texts.3: SP arrived over Zero Point with all required procedures already complete and the aircraft established at the planned altitude, airspeed and heading. The navigation setup, the checks and the timing reference were in place before the point. The transition from the departure to the first leg required no additional action.
texts.4: SP had every required procedure complete well before Zero Point and crossed it exactly at the planned parameters. Cockpit work was sequenced so that the final segment of the departure was flown with full capacity available for flying the aircraft. The transition to the route was made without any interruption of the profile.
texts.marginal: SP completed the required procedures before Zero Point, but the last items were closed only in the final seconds of the departure segment. Nothing was omitted, yet the margin left no room to absorb any interruption. SP is expected to begin the sequence earlier so that Zero Point is reached with the cockpit work already closed.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the required procedures before Zero Point with IP naming each remaining item and confirming the aircraft is established at the point, due to this being one of the first departures SP has sequenced to have every procedure complete before a specific point. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to complete more of the sequence independently before Zero Point on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP arrived over Zero Point with the required procedures complete, at the edge of the standard, due to the last item being closed only in the final seconds before the point rather than earlier in the sequence. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to close the last item earlier in the sequence, not in the final seconds.
texts_at.2: SP arrived over Zero Point with the required procedures complete, due to one item being actioned a beat later in the sequence than the rest. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to action every item at the same point in the sequence, not one item late.
texts_at.3: SP arrived over Zero Point with the required procedures complete, due to the sequence being begun a fraction later than it could have been despite finishing in good time. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the sequence a fraction earlier so the margin at the point grows.

texts_above.1: SP arrived over Zero Point with the required procedures complete, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP arrived over Zero Point with all required procedures already complete and the aircraft established at the planned altitude, airspeed and heading, the navigation setup and the timing reference in place before the point. Beginning the sequence a fraction earlier still would leave a wider margin at the point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pre-point sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP had every required procedure complete well before Zero Point, crossing it exactly at the planned parameters with cockpit work sequenced so the final segment of the departure was flown with full capacity available. The only refinement available was to widen that same margin by a few more seconds. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate pre-point sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP had every required procedure complete well before Zero Point and crossed it exactly at the planned parameters, cockpit work sequenced so the final segment of the departure was flown with full capacity available for flying the aircraft and the transition to the route made without any interruption. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary pre-point sequencing.

error_modes.label: Compliance with the published departure sequence and restrictions

texts.0: SP, due to a departure procedure that had not been reviewed against the published plate, did not fly the prescribed sequence of the SID and did not turn at a required point. The aircraft continued past the segment limit with no correcting action. The IP intervened to re-establish the aircraft on the published departure.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the departure sequence, did not initiate the next segment at the published point and continued straight beyond it. The turn was started only after the IP prompted the segment change. The published track was rejoined late, with the heading error at the 10 degree limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to late identification of the segment change point, did not begin the turn exactly at the published position and overshot the following track. SP recognized the error against the navigation display and regained the published departure track without prompting. The remaining segments were flown in the correct sequence and within the restrictions.
texts.3: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID in the published sequence, initiating each segment at the correct point. The altitude and speed restrictions of the departure were met at each fix. The published ground track was maintained throughout the procedure.
texts.4: SP executed the departure exactly as published, initiating each segment at the correct point and meeting every restriction with margin. Anticipation of the turn points kept the aircraft on the published track with no corrections required. The complete departure was flown without any input from the IP.
texts.marginal: SP flew the departure in the correct sequence, but each segment change was initiated at the latest acceptable moment. The restrictions were met, yet with little margin at the fixes. SP is expected to anticipate the turn points so that the published track is flown without late corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the SID sequence with IP calling each segment change point and confirming the restriction at each fix, due to this being one of the first SIDs SP has flown from the published segment points rather than from a talked-through route. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to identify more of the segment change points independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP initiated each segment of the SID at the published point, holding the heading error to about 10 degrees at the segment change, at the edge of the standard, due to the change point being identified only as it was reached rather than anticipated before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to anticipate the segment change point rather than identifying it as it is reached.
texts_at.2: SP initiated each segment of the SID at the published point, holding the heading error to about 7 degrees at the segment change, due to the navigation display being checked a beat after the turn should have begun. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the navigation display before the turn is due, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP initiated each segment of the SID at the published point, holding the heading error to about 5 degrees at the segment change, due to the turn being started a fraction later than the earliest acceptable point. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to start each turn at the earliest acceptable point, not a fraction later.

texts_above.1: SP initiated each segment of the SID at the published point, holding the heading error to about 9 degrees at the segment change, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID in the published sequence, holding the heading error to about 7 degrees at each segment change with the altitude and speed restrictions met with margin. Starting each turn at the earliest acceptable point, rather than a fraction later, would widen the margin at every fix. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable published-sequence discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the VFR departure and the SID in the published sequence, holding the heading error to about 4 degrees at each segment change with the published ground track maintained throughout the procedure. The only refinement available was to hold that same margin through the single tightest restriction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good published-sequence discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed the departure exactly as published, initiating each segment at the correct point and meeting every restriction with margin, anticipation of the turn points keeping the aircraft on the published track with no corrections required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior published-sequence discipline.

error_modes.label: Departure clearance handling and radio communication

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not read back the departure clearance correctly and flew a route other than the one issued. The discrepancy was not detected in the cockpit and the aircraft continued off the cleared departure. The IP intervened to clarify with the controller and to correct the aircraft track.
texts.1: SP, due to a read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, did not act on the departure instruction as issued and began the wrong segment. The discrepancy was resolved only after the IP prompted a query to the controller. Compliance was restored after a delay during which the aircraft remained off the cleared route.
texts.2: SP, due to a read-back made before the transmission had been fully received, did not initially confirm the correct departure instruction. SP requested a repeat, corrected the read-back and complied with the clearance without any intervention. The remainder of the departure was flown as cleared.
texts.3: SP read back the departure clearance completely and in standard phraseology, and complied with it as issued. The required calls were made at the briefed points without blocking other transmissions. Changes to the clearance were acknowledged and translated into the flown profile correctly.
texts.4: SP handled all departure communications in standard phraseology with complete and accurate read-backs. Clearances and amendments were acknowledged immediately and reflected in the flight path without delay. Radio work was managed with no effect on the accuracy of the flown parameters.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the departure clearance and made the required calls, but several transmissions were incomplete and had to be prompted by the controller. Comprehension was correct, yet the phraseology was not consistently standard. SP is expected to use complete standard read-backs so that intent is unambiguous to the controller.

texts_at.0: SP copied and read back the departure clearance with IP confirming each element against the issued clearance, due to this being one of the first departure clearances SP has copied and read back without a rehearsed script. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to read back more of the clearance independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP read back the departure clearance and complied with it as issued, due to one transmission being completed only after the controller prompted for the missing element. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete every transmission the first time, not after a prompt.
texts_at.2: SP read back the departure clearance and complied with it as issued, due to one read-back being built from memory of the filed plan before it was checked against the actual clearance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check every read-back against the actual clearance, not memory of the filed plan.
texts_at.3: SP read back the departure clearance and complied with it as issued, due to one call being phrased a fraction less standard than the rest before it was corrected. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to phrase every call to the same standard as the rest, from the first transmission.

texts_above.1: SP read back the departure clearance and complied with it as issued. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP read back the departure clearance completely and in standard phraseology and complied with it as issued, the required calls made at the briefed points without blocking other transmissions. Phrasing every call to the same standard from the first transmission would remove the one prompt needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured clearance-readback discipline.
texts_above.3: SP read back the departure clearance completely and in standard phraseology, with changes to the clearance acknowledged and translated into the flown profile correctly and no transmission requiring IP intervention. The only refinement available was to hold that same standard phraseology through the busiest radio segment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise clearance-readback discipline.
texts_above.4: SP handled all departure communications in standard phraseology with complete and accurate read-backs, clearances and amendments acknowledged immediately and reflected in the flight path without delay with radio work managed with no effect on the accuracy of the flown parameters. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate clearance-readback discipline.

error_modes.label: After-takeoff configuration changes, trim and power management

texts.0: SP, due to an omitted step in the after-takeoff sequence, did not retract the gear and flaps at the scheduled points and entered the departure climb with the aircraft still configured. The additional drag was compensated with pitch instead of with the correct configuration and the climb schedule was not achieved. The IP intervened to complete the configuration change.
texts.1: SP, due to attention concentrated on capturing the departure heading, did not complete the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points and left the aircraft out of trim through the initial climb. The items were completed only after the IP called for them. The aircraft was flown with continuous control pressure until the trim was finally set.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed trim input after flap retraction, did not relieve the control pressure immediately and allowed a small pitch excursion to develop in the climb. SP recognized the condition, trimmed the aircraft and re-established the climb attitude without prompting. The rest of the departure was flown in trim.
texts.3: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points and trimmed the aircraft for the departure climb. Power was set to the briefed climb value and no residual control pressure was carried into the turns. Aircraft handling supported accurate parameter keeping throughout the departure.
texts.4: SP sequenced the configuration changes, power and trim so precisely that the departure climb showed no transient at any point. The aircraft was in trim at every stage, leaving full capacity for the navigation and radio tasks. Power management matched the briefed profile exactly.
texts.marginal: SP completed the configuration changes and trimmed the aircraft, but each trim input followed its configuration change later than it should have. Control of the aircraft was never in question, yet residual pressures were carried briefly into each segment. SP is expected to trim immediately after each configuration change.

texts_at.0: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes with IP calling the scheduled points and confirming the trim alongside SP, due to this being one of the first departures SP has sequenced gear, flap and trim changes to a scheduled point rather than a called cue. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to sequence more of the configuration changes independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points, holding the resulting airspeed to about 20 knots inside the standard, at the edge of the standard, due to the trim input following the flap retraction by a beat rather than in the same motion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim in the same motion as the configuration change, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points, holding the resulting airspeed to about 15 knots inside the standard, due to a delayed trim input allowing a small pitch excursion before it was corrected. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to trim before the pitch excursion develops, not after it.
texts_at.3: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points, holding the resulting airspeed to about 10 knots inside the standard, due to a control pressure being relieved a fraction after the configuration change rather than with it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to relieve the control pressure in the same motion as the configuration change.

texts_above.1: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points, holding the resulting airspeed to about 18 knots inside the standard, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP completed the after-takeoff configuration changes at the scheduled points and trimmed the aircraft for the departure climb, holding airspeed to about 15 knots inside the standard with no residual control pressure carried into the turns. Relieving the control pressure in the same motion as the configuration change, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent configuration-trim discipline.
texts_above.3: SP sequenced the configuration changes, power and trim so the departure climb showed only about 8 knots of transient at any point, leaving capacity for the navigation and radio tasks. The only refinement available was to hold that same sequencing through the busiest configuration change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined configuration-trim discipline.
texts_above.4: SP sequenced the configuration changes, power and trim so precisely that the departure climb showed no transient at any point, the aircraft in trim at every stage with power management matching the briefed profile exactly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless configuration-trim discipline.

error_modes.label: Outside lookout and position awareness in the VFR departure corridor

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft position relative to the departure corridor, did not maintain the outside lookout required in VMC and did not identify the lateral limits of the departure area. The aircraft approached the corridor boundary with no correcting action. The IP intervened to turn the aircraft back inside the published area.
texts.1: SP, due to attention fixed inside the cockpit on the navigation display, did not sustain the outside scan during the VFR departure and did not confirm the planned visual references. Position awareness was restored only after the IP pointed out the reference. The planned track was regained after a delay, with the heading error at the 10 degree limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan biased toward the instruments during the initial climb, did not identify the first visual reference at the expected time. SP re-established the outside scan, positively identified the reference and confirmed the aircraft position against the plan without prompting. Terrain and airspace clearance were maintained throughout.
texts.3: SP maintained an effective outside scan during the VFR departure while sustaining the instrument cross-check. Visual references were identified at the planned points and the aircraft was kept clear of terrain and of the airspace limits. Traffic in the departure area was seen and called.
texts.4: SP divided attention between the outside scan and the cockpit tasks with no degradation to either. Every visual reference was identified early and the aircraft position was known continuously relative to the airspace and the terrain. Traffic was acquired and deconflicted with no effect on the flown parameters.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft clear of terrain and of the airspace limits, but the outside scan was interrupted for long periods while cockpit tasks were worked. The visual references were identified, though later than planned. SP is expected to shorten the head-down periods so that the outside picture is maintained continuously.

texts_at.0: SP divided attention between the outside lookout and the cockpit tasks with IP calling when to return the scan outside, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown dividing attention between an outside scan and cockpit work in the corridor. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to return more of the scan outside independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the outside lookout with the departure heading held to about 10 degrees during the busiest cockpit task, at the edge of the standard, due to one head-down period running long enough that the outside picture had to be rebuilt afterward. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten every head-down period so the outside picture never needs rebuilding.

texts_at.3: SP maintained the outside lookout with the departure heading held to about 5 degrees during the busiest cockpit task, due to one head-down period running a fraction longer than the rest before the scan returned outside. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold every head-down period to the same short length as the rest.

texts_above.3: SP maintained an effective outside scan during the VFR departure while sustaining the instrument cross-check, the departure heading held to about 4 degrees with the aircraft kept clear of terrain and of the airspace limits and traffic seen and called. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent scan-division discipline.

error_modes.label: First turn after takeoff before the departure end of the runway and below the 140 KIAS / 700 feet AGL gate

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started before passing the departure end of the runway, did not climb straight ahead as required and rolled into the departure turn below 140 KIAS and below 700 feet AGL. Airspeed at roll-in was more than 20 knots below the climb schedule and the aircraft was more than 300 feet below the departure profile. The IP intervened to roll out and re-establish the straight ahead climb before the turn was resumed.
texts.1: SP, due to anticipation of the departure track, did not delay the first turn until past the departure end of the runway and initiated it while 140 KIAS was still being attained. Airspeed at roll-in sat 20 knots low and the altitude at the turn reached 300 feet below the departure profile, the outer limit of the standard. The bank was reduced only after the IP called for wings level until the minimum turn parameters were met.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll-in begun abeam rather than past the departure end of the runway, did not fully attain the 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL gate before the first turn. Airspeed at roll-in was about 15 knots below schedule and the aircraft was some 200 feet low on the profile. SP recognized the shortfall, shallowed the bank and re-established the climb schedule inside 10 knots without any prompt.
texts.3: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway and started the first turn only after 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL were attained. Airspeed and altitude at roll-in stayed inside 10 knots and 150 feet of the departure profile. Bank was applied smoothly so that the rate of climb was preserved through the turn.
texts.4: SP held the straight ahead climb well past the departure end of the runway and initiated the first turn with the 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL gate comfortably met. Deviations from the climb schedule at roll-in were negligible on both the airspeed indicator and the altimeter. The turn was entered at the exact point required by local directives with no loss of climb performance.
texts.marginal: SP met the 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL gate before the first turn, but the roll-in was consistently started at the earliest acceptable point rather than with margin. Parameters stayed inside the standard, although the sequence left no room for a distraction during the initial climb. SP is expected to confirm both the departure end of the runway and the minimum turn parameters before applying bank.

texts_at.0: SP climbed straight ahead after takeoff with IP calling when both the airspeed and the altitude gates were met before the first turn, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown confirming two separate gates before turning rather than one visual cue. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to confirm more of both gates independently before the roll-in on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway before turning, with airspeed at roll-in held to about 18 knots and altitude to about 280 feet of the departure profile, at the edge of the standard, due to both gates being confirmed only as the roll-in began rather than before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm both gates before the roll-in begins, not as it begins.
texts_at.2: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway before turning, with airspeed at roll-in held to about 15 knots and altitude to about 200 feet of the departure profile, due to the bank being applied a beat before the second gate was fully confirmed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm both gates fully before any bank is applied.
texts_at.3: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway before turning, with airspeed at roll-in held to about 8 knots and altitude to about 130 feet of the departure profile, due to the confirmation of both gates coming a fraction later than the earliest possible point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm both gates at the earliest possible point, not a fraction later.

texts_above.1: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway before turning, with airspeed at roll-in held to about 18 knots and altitude to about 280 feet of the departure profile, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway and started the first turn only after 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL were attained, airspeed and altitude at roll-in held to about 15 knots and 200 feet of the departure profile. Confirming both gates at the earliest possible point, rather than a fraction later, would build in a wider margin. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sound departure-gate discipline.
texts_above.3: SP climbed straight ahead well past the departure end of the runway before turning, airspeed and altitude at roll-in held to about 8 knots and 130 feet of the departure profile with bank applied smoothly so the rate of climb was preserved through the turn. The only refinement available was to build that same margin into a shorter runway. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sure-handed departure-gate discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the straight ahead climb well past the departure end of the runway and initiated the first turn with the minimum turn parameters comfortably met, deviations from the climb schedule at roll-in negligible on both the airspeed indicator and the altimeter with the turn entered at the exact point required by local directives with no loss of climb performance. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional departure-gate discipline.

error_modes.label: Climbout flown below 160 KIAS with a high pitch attitude that limits forward visibility

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude set well above the 10-15 degree climb reference, did not accelerate to the 140-180 KIAS climb schedule and stabilized the climbout more than 20 knots below the briefed climb airspeed. The nose-high attitude limited forward visibility to the extent that the departure references could not be acquired and the track was not maintained. The IP intervened to lower the nose and restore the climb schedule.
texts.1: SP, due to a climb attitude carried high after takeoff, did not lower the nose to the airspeed required and climbed out 20 knots below the briefed value, at the outer limit of the standard. Forward visibility over the nose was reduced to the point that the departure references were identified late. The correction followed only after the IP prompted an airspeed check.
texts.2: SP, due to a climb attitude set nearer 15 degrees than the airspeed called for, did not hold the briefed climbout airspeed and allowed it to decay about 15 knots low. SP noted the trend on the airspeed indicator, lowered the nose toward the attitude that produces the briefed airspeed and regained the schedule inside 10 knots without prompting. Forward visibility for the departure references was restored before the first turn.
texts.3: SP flew the climbout at the briefed airspeed within the 140-180 KIAS band and kept it inside 10 knots throughout the departure climb. Pitch was held in the 10-15 degree range so that forward visibility over the nose remained adequate for the departure references. The climb schedule was not allowed to settle below 160 KIAS.
texts.4: SP established the climbout airspeed immediately after takeoff and held it with negligible variation for the whole departure climb. Pitch was set from the airspeed required, so the attitude never grew high enough to restrict the view over the nose. The climb gradient matched the planned departure profile exactly.
texts.marginal: SP kept the climbout airspeed inside the standard, but it settled repeatedly toward the low end near 160 KIAS with a correspondingly high pitch attitude. Forward visibility remained usable, although the margin for identifying the departure references was thin. SP is expected to set pitch from the airspeed required rather than accepting the higher attitude.

texts_at.0: SP flew the climbout with IP calling the pitch attitude needed to reach the briefed airspeed, due to this being one of the first climbouts SP has flown setting pitch from the airspeed required rather than by feel. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to set more of the climb pitch independently from the airspeed required on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP flew the climbout at about 20 knots below the briefed value, at the edge of the standard, due to the pitch attitude being carried high after takeoff before it was lowered toward the airspeed required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lower the pitch toward the airspeed required immediately after takeoff, not after it is carried high.
texts_at.2: SP flew the climbout at about 15 knots below the briefed value, due to the climb attitude being set nearer the steep end of the range than the airspeed called for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the climb attitude from the airspeed called for, not the steep end of the range.
texts_at.3: SP flew the climbout at about 10 knots below the briefed value, due to the nose being lowered a fraction after the trend was noticed rather than as it was noticed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lower the nose in the same instant the trend is noticed.

texts_above.1: SP flew the climbout at about 18 knots below the briefed value, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew the climbout at the briefed airspeed to about 15 knots, pitch held in the range that keeps forward visibility adequate for the departure references with the climb schedule not allowed to settle below 160 KIAS. Lowering the nose in the same instant the trend is noticed, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid climbout-pitch discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the climbout at the briefed airspeed to about 8 knots, pitch set from the airspeed required so forward visibility over the nose remained clear for the departure references throughout. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through a heavier aircraft weight. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed climbout-pitch discipline.
texts_above.4: SP established the climbout airspeed immediately after takeoff and held it with negligible variation for the whole departure climb, pitch set from the airspeed required so the attitude never grew high enough to restrict the view over the nose with the climb gradient matching the planned departure profile exactly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding climbout-pitch discipline.

error_modes.label: Level-off lead point at departure altitude restrictions (10 % of VSI technique)

texts.0: SP, due to a level-off begun without any lead point, did not start lowering the nose before reaching the assigned departure altitude and let the established rate of climb carry the aircraft through it. The overshoot passed 300 feet and was still increasing when the IP intervened to establish level flight. The recovery placed the aircraft outside the altitude restriction of that departure segment.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead point far smaller than the 10 % of VSI technique requires, did not begin the transition early enough and overshot the level-off altitude by 300 feet, the outer limit of the standard. The nose was lowered only after the IP called the altitude. Level flight and the briefed airspeed were re-established well beyond the point required by the departure.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead point taken from a rate of climb that had already increased, did not lead the capture sufficiently and overshot the assigned altitude by about 200 feet. SP recognized the overshoot on the altimeter and returned the aircraft inside 150 feet with a smooth correction and no prompt. The following level-off was led correctly.
texts.3: SP started each level-off at a lead point of approximately 10 % of the VSI and captured the assigned altitude within 150 feet. The nose was lowered smoothly to level flight, the PCL was then adjusted to the desired airspeed and the aircraft was trimmed. No overshoot developed at any departure altitude restriction.
texts.4: SP sized every lead point from the actual rate of climb and captured each altitude with no measurable overshoot. The transition from climb to level flight was smooth, with power and trim set as the airspeed settled. The altitude restrictions of the departure were met without any subsequent correction being required.
texts.marginal: SP led each level-off and stayed inside the standard, but the lead points used were smaller than the rate of climb called for and each capture ended with a small overshoot. Altitude control was never in doubt, yet the pattern depended on a late correction every time. SP is expected to size the lead point from the actual VSI before beginning the level-off.

texts_at.0: SP flew the level-off with IP calling the lead point sized from the rate of climb, due to this being one of the first level-offs SP has flown sizing the lead point from the 10 percent of VSI technique rather than a called altitude. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to size more of the lead point independently from the rate of climb on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP captured the assigned altitude to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the lead point being sized smaller than the actual rate of climb called for. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size the lead point from the actual rate of climb, not a smaller figure.
texts_at.2: SP captured the assigned altitude to about 210 feet, due to the lead point being taken from a rate of climb that had already increased rather than the current one. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to take the lead point from the current rate of climb, not an earlier one.
texts_at.3: SP captured the assigned altitude to about 120 feet, due to the nose being lowered a fraction after the lead point rather than exactly at it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lower the nose exactly at the lead point, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP captured the assigned altitude to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP started each level-off at a lead point of approximately 10 percent of the VSI and captured the assigned altitude to about 200 feet, the nose lowered smoothly to level flight with no overshoot at any restriction. Lowering the nose exactly at the lead point, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the capture further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady level-off lead discipline.
texts_above.3: SP started each level-off at a lead point sized from the actual rate of climb and captured the assigned altitude to about 130 feet, power and trim set as the airspeed settled with no subsequent correction required. The only refinement available was to size that same lead point through the steepest rate of climb of the departure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate level-off lead discipline.
texts_above.4: SP sized every lead point from the actual rate of climb and captured each altitude with no measurable overshoot, the transition from climb to level flight smooth with the altitude restrictions of the departure met without any subsequent correction required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary level-off lead discipline.

error_modes.label: Pitch, bank and heading flown on instruments instead of outside references cross-checked with the EHSI

texts.0: SP, due to pitch and bank changes made on the instruments while outside references were available, did not use section lines or a prominent point near the horizon to hold the departure climb and flew the whole segment head-down. Heading wandered more than 10 degrees from the departure track and the wings-level attitude was not maintained between crosschecks. The IP intervened to direct the attention outside and re-establish the track.
texts.1: SP, due to a crosscheck built on the attitude indicator rather than on outside references, did not fly the climb attitude visually and allowed the departure heading to reach 10 degrees of error, the limit of the standard. Outside references were used only after the IP directed the attention outside the cockpit. Wings-level attitude was thereafter confirmed against the horizon rather than the instruments.
texts.2: SP, due to pitch changes initiated on the instruments before the horizon was used, did not hold the climb attitude steadily and let the departure heading open to about 7 degrees. SP shifted the crosscheck to a ground reference near the horizon, confirmed it on the EHSI and closed the error inside 5 degrees unprompted. The remainder of the climb was flown on outside references.
texts.3: SP made all pitch and bank changes using outside references and crosschecked heading on the EHSI and wings level on the attitude indicator. The departure heading was held within 5 degrees and the climb attitude remained stable. The instruments were used to confirm the outside picture rather than to replace it.
texts.4: SP flew the entire departure climb from the outside picture, using section lines and a prominent point near the horizon, with the EHSI and attitude indicator serving only as confirmation. Heading and attitude deviations remained negligible throughout. The crosscheck rhythm left ample capacity for clearing and for the departure radio work.
texts.marginal: SP used outside references for the climb attitude, but the crosscheck reverted to the instruments whenever a correction was needed and the head-down periods lengthened. Heading and attitude stayed inside the standard, though the outside picture was not continuously maintained. SP is expected to initiate corrections visually and confirm them on the EHSI rather than the reverse.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure climb with IP calling the outside references to use for pitch and bank and confirming them against the EHSI, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown using outside references as the primary picture rather than the instruments. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to initiate more of the corrections from outside references independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the departure heading to about 10 degrees using outside references, at the edge of the standard, due to one correction being initiated on the instruments before it was confirmed against the outside picture. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to initiate every correction visually and confirm it on the EHSI, not the reverse.
texts_at.2: SP held the departure heading to about 7 degrees using outside references, due to a pitch change being initiated on the instruments a beat before the horizon was used to refine it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to initiate every pitch change from the horizon, not the instruments.
texts_at.3: SP held the departure heading to about 5 degrees using outside references, due to the crosscheck shifting to a ground reference a fraction after the correction rather than in the same motion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to shift the crosscheck to the ground reference in the same motion as the correction.

texts_above.1: SP held the departure heading to about 9 degrees using outside references, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP made all pitch and bank changes using outside references and crosschecked heading on the EHSI, the departure heading held to about 7 degrees with the instruments used to confirm the outside picture rather than replace it. Shifting the crosscheck to the ground reference in the same motion as the correction, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the technique further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to dependable outside-reference discipline.
texts_above.3: SP made all pitch and bank changes using outside references, the departure heading held to about 4 degrees with the climb attitude remaining stable throughout. The only refinement available was to hold that same outside-reference discipline through the busiest part of the climb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to notably good outside-reference discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entire departure climb from the outside picture, using section lines and a prominent point near the horizon with the EHSI and attitude indicator serving only as confirmation, heading and attitude deviations remaining negligible throughout with the crosscheck rhythm leaving ample capacity for clearing and the departure radio work. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior outside-reference discipline.

error_modes.label: Climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and operations check at initial level-off

texts.0: SP, due to attention held on the departure track, did not initiate the climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and did not conduct the operations check at initial level-off. The aircraft was flown through the departure with the systems and fuel state unverified, and altitude keeping degraded past 300 feet while the omission was addressed. The IP intervened to direct both checks and to restore the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a crosscheck that did not include the altimeter as a trigger, did not initiate the climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and completed it well into the next departure segment. Altitude deviation reached 300 feet while the check was being run, at the outer limit of the standard. The operations check at initial level-off was carried out only after the IP called for it.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed transition from the climb to the level-off task, did not start the operations check at initial level-off and ran it late in the segment, letting the altitude drift about 200 feet. SP recognized the drift, stabilized the aircraft inside 150 feet and completed the check without prompting. The climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL had been accomplished at the correct point.
texts.3: SP initiated the climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and conducted the operations check at initial level-off as required by the flight manual. Altitude was held within 150 feet while both checks were run. The checks were then repeated periodically without interfering with the departure navigation.
texts.4: SP triggered the climb check exactly at 10.000 feet MSL and the operations check immediately at initial level-off, with no measurable effect on altitude or heading. Both checks were completed while the departure track and the outside scan were maintained. The periodic repetition of the operations check was equally well timed.
texts.marginal: SP accomplished both the climb check and the operations check, but each was started noticeably after its trigger and produced a small altitude excursion within the standard. The content of the checks was complete and correct. SP is expected to treat 10.000 feet MSL and initial level-off as firm triggers rather than as approximate cues.

texts_at.0: SP ran the climb check and the operations check with IP calling the trigger altitude and the initial level-off as the cue for each, due to this being one of the first departures SP has flown triggering both checks from a specific altitude rather than from a reminder. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to trigger more of both checks independently from the altitude cue on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude, holding the resulting altitude deviation to about 300 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the trigger being treated as an approximate cue rather than a firm one. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to treat the altitude trigger as firm, not as an approximate cue.
texts_at.2: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude, holding the resulting altitude deviation to about 210 feet, due to the transition from the climb task to the level-off task being made a beat after the trigger. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to make the transition to the level-off task exactly at the trigger.
texts_at.3: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude, holding the resulting altitude deviation to about 150 feet, due to the operations check starting a fraction after initial level-off rather than at it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to start the operations check exactly at initial level-off, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude, holding the resulting altitude deviation to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude and conducted the operations check at initial level-off, altitude held to about 200 feet while both checks were run with the checks repeated periodically without interfering with the navigation. Starting the operations check exactly at initial level-off, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured check-trigger discipline.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the climb check at the trigger altitude and conducted the operations check at initial level-off, altitude held to about 130 feet while both checks were completed with the departure track and the outside scan maintained. The only refinement available was to treat that same trigger as firm through a faster rate of climb. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise check-trigger discipline.
texts_above.4: SP triggered the climb check exactly at the prescribed altitude and the operations check immediately at initial level-off, with no measurable effect on altitude or heading, both checks completed while the departure track and the outside scan were maintained with the periodic repetition equally well timed. error_modes.label: Trim and stabilization on heading and altitude toward the first checkpoint

texts.0: SP, due to poor trim carried through the level-off, did not stabilize the aircraft on the heading and altitude toward the first checkpoint and flew the leg against continuous control pressure. Altitude wandered beyond 300 feet and the heading beyond 10 degrees, and fuel flow was uneven as power was repeatedly readjusted. The IP intervened to trim the aircraft and re-establish the leg to the first checkpoint.
texts.1: SP, due to trim not being reset after the level-off, did not achieve the stabilized cruise condition toward the first checkpoint and held the aircraft with control pressure throughout. Altitude and heading errors reached 300 feet and 10 degrees, the outer limits of the standard, and the workload consumed the capacity needed for the navigation crosscheck. The aircraft was finally trimmed only after the IP prompted it.
texts.2: SP, due to trim applied in one coarse input rather than refined after the airspeed settled, did not stabilize fully on the leg and allowed a 200 feet altitude drift and a heading error of about 7 degrees. SP recognized the residual pressure, retrimmed in pitch and rudder and stabilized inside 150 feet and 5 degrees without prompting. The leg to the first checkpoint was then flown hands-light.
texts.3: SP levelled off using normal procedures and trimmed the aircraft so that it was stabilized on heading and altitude to the first checkpoint. Altitude was held within 150 feet and heading within 5 degrees with light control forces. Cruise control was set so that fuel flow remained even for the leg.
texts.4: SP trimmed the aircraft precisely after the level-off and stabilized on the heading and altitude to the first checkpoint immediately. Deviations remained negligible and the aircraft required essentially no control pressure to hold the leg. The resulting low workload left full capacity for the visual navigation crosscheck.
texts.marginal: SP trimmed the aircraft and reached a stabilized condition toward the first checkpoint, but only after several corrections and later than the level-off allowed. Altitude and heading stayed inside the standard while the trim was being refined. SP is expected to trim as the airspeed settles at level-off so that the leg starts already stabilized.

texts_at.0: SP levelled off toward the first checkpoint with IP calling the trim needed to stabilize on the assigned heading and altitude, due to this being one of the first level-offs SP has flown trimming for a stabilized cruise toward a named checkpoint. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to trim more of the level-off independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized on the heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, holding altitude to about 280 feet and heading to about 9 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the trim being refined over several corrections rather than set once as the airspeed settled. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim once as the airspeed settles, not through several corrections.
texts_at.2: SP stabilized on the heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, holding altitude to about 210 feet and heading to about 7 degrees, due to the trim input being coarse and needing a refinement a beat later rather than being set precisely the first time. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set the trim precisely the first time, not coarsely with a later refinement.
texts_at.3: SP stabilized on the heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, holding altitude to about 120 feet and heading to about 4 degrees, due to the residual control pressure being recognized a fraction after level-off rather than at it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to recognize any residual pressure at level-off itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized on the heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, holding altitude to about 280 feet and heading to about 9 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP levelled off using normal procedures and trimmed the aircraft so it was stabilized on heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, altitude held to about 200 feet and heading to about 7 degrees with light control forces. Recognizing any residual pressure at level-off itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the stabilization further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent post-level-off stabilization.
texts_above.3: SP levelled off using normal procedures and trimmed the aircraft so it was stabilized on heading and altitude to the first checkpoint, altitude held to about 130 feet and heading to about 4 degrees with cruise control set so fuel flow remained even. The only refinement available was to hold that same stabilization through a faster climb rate. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined post-level-off stabilization.
