error_modes.label: Departure routing, altitude restrictions and NAVAID / GPS setup completed before takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to departure routing and altitude restrictions not being reviewed before takeoff and the NAVAIDs and GPS left unset, did not have the departure available when the clearance was issued and attempted to build it airborne. The head-down work displaced aircraft control and the assigned altitude and track were both exceeded past the code 1 limits. The IP intervened to fly the aircraft and to establish it on the published departure.
texts.1: SP, due to preferred routings not being planned, did not anticipate the route change contained in the clearance and had to set the NAVAIDs and GPS during the initial climb. Altitude reached 300 feet from the assigned value and the departure track opened to 10 degrees while the setup was completed. The situation was resolved only after the IP prompted a return to the assigned parameters.
texts.2: SP, due to a partial NAVAID and GPS setup before takeoff, did not have one of the departure restrictions loaded and reconstructed it after the first turn, letting the altitude drift about 200 feet. SP prioritized aircraft control, completed the setup and returned inside 150 feet and 5 degrees without prompting. The remainder of the departure was flown as published.
texts.3: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, with the approach plate for the departure airfield readily available. The departure was flown as cleared with altitude within 150 feet and track within 5 degrees. The pre-takeoff preparation absorbed the clearance detail without airborne reconfiguration.
texts.4: SP planned the preferred routings, reviewed the departure restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS completely before takeoff, keeping the approach plate accessible for an emergency return. The issued clearance required no airborne reconfiguration and the departure was flown with negligible deviations. Situational awareness was maintained through every routing and altitude restriction.
texts.marginal: SP set the NAVAIDs and GPS and reviewed the departure before takeoff, but the review was thin enough that parts of the clearance had to be confirmed during the climb. Parameters stayed inside the standard while this was done. SP is expected to plan preferred routings and complete the departure review so that no reconstruction is needed airborne.

texts_at.0: SP reviewed the departure routing and set the NAVAIDs and GPS with IP naming each restriction to confirm before takeoff, due to this being one of the first departures SP has prepared setting up the NAVAIDs and GPS for the full published routing before taxi. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to confirm more of the routing and restrictions independently before takeoff on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, holding altitude to about 300 feet and track to about 10 degrees while confirming one clearance element during the climb, at the edge of the standard, due to the pre-takeoff review being thin enough that the element needed reconstruction airborne. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to review every clearance element before takeoff so none needs reconstruction airborne.
texts_at.2: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, holding altitude to about 210 feet and track to about 7 degrees while confirming one clearance element during the climb, due to the preferred routing not being planned for that segment. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to plan the preferred routing for every segment, not only the ones most likely to change.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, holding altitude to about 120 feet and track to about 4 degrees, due to one restriction being confirmed a fraction later than the rest of the review. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm every restriction to the same depth as the rest of the review.

texts_above.1: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, holding altitude to about 280 feet and track to about 9 degrees while confirming one clearance element during the climb, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, altitude held to about 200 feet and track to about 7 degrees with the pre-takeoff preparation absorbing the clearance detail without airborne reconfiguration. Confirming every restriction to the same depth as the rest of the review would remove the last airborne reconstruction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to good pre-takeoff review discipline.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS before takeoff, altitude held to about 130 feet and track to about 4 degrees with situational awareness maintained through every routing and altitude restriction. The only refinement available was to hold that same depth of review through a last-minute clearance change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to very good pre-takeoff review discipline.
texts_above.4: SP planned the preferred routings, reviewed the departure restrictions and set the NAVAIDs and GPS completely before takeoff, keeping the approach plate accessible for an emergency return, the issued clearance requiring no airborne reconfiguration with the departure flown with negligible deviations. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent pre-takeoff review discipline.

error_modes.label: Overtake and separation control on the rejoin following a formation departure

texts.0: SP, due to failure to recognize excessive overtake, did not compare actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed and closed on Number 1 far above the 20-30 KIAS of planned closure. Lateral and vertical separation were not maintained until the closure rate was under control and the aircraft arrived in route with unmanaged aspect. The IP intervened to arrest the closure and re-establish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to bank and overtake not being monitored during the last few hundred feet, did not begin the power reduction at the critical stage of the rejoin and carried closure more than 20 knots above the rejoin airspeed past the rejoin's briefed altitude gate. The aspect reference was lost and the arrival in route was made without stabilized closure. The correction was applied only after the IP called the overtake.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction started later than the rejoin's briefed altitude gate, did not decrease closure in time and reached the route position with about 15 knots of overtake. SP maintained vertical separation with Number 1 held two to four ship widths from the horizon, used the speed brake below 20 percent torque and stabilized co-airspeed without prompting. The move into fingertip was then made at a controlled rate.
texts.3: SP flew the rejoin with the planned 20-30 KIAS of closure and kept the vertical stabilizer bisecting the outside wing as the aspect reference. Closure was reduced with power inside 500 feet so that the route position was reached within 10 knots of Number 1. Lateral and vertical separation were maintained until the closure rate was fully under control.
texts.4: SP managed aspect with small bank adjustments and reduced closure so precisely that the route position was reached co-airspeed with Number 1 and no line-of-sight rate. Separation was never in question at any stage of the rejoin. The transition into fingertip was smooth and made only after the aircraft was stabilized in route.
texts.marginal: SP completed the rejoin inside the standard, but closure was reduced later than the critical stage of the rejoin required and the last correction was sizeable. Separation was maintained throughout and the arrival in route was safe. SP is expected to compare actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed earlier so that overtake is bled off before 500 feet.

texts_at.0: SP flew the rejoin toward Number 1 with IP calling the power reduction at the rejoin's briefed altitude gate and confirming the closure, due to this being one of the first rejoins SP has flown managing overtake against a specific airspeed and altitude gate. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin more of the power reduction independently at the briefed gate on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP flew the rejoin with about 20 knots of overtake still to bleed off inside the critical range, at the edge of the planned closure, due to the comparison against the directed rejoin airspeed being made only as the critical stage was reached rather than before it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compare against the directed rejoin airspeed before the critical stage, not as it is reached.
texts_at.2: SP flew the rejoin with about 15 knots of overtake still to bleed off inside the critical range, due to the power reduction beginning a beat after the critical stage rather than at it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the power reduction at the critical stage itself, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP flew the rejoin with about 10 knots of overtake still to bleed off inside the critical range, due to the aspect reference being confirmed a fraction after the bank was adjusted rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the aspect reference in the same motion as the bank adjustment.

texts_above.1: SP flew the rejoin with about 20 knots of overtake still to bleed off inside the critical range, at the edge of the planned closure. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew the rejoin with the planned 20 to 30 KIAS of closure and kept the vertical stabilizer bisecting the outside wing as the aspect reference, reducing closure with power inside the critical range so route position was reached with about 10 knots of overtake remaining. Confirming the aspect reference in the same motion as the bank adjustment, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the closure control further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound rejoin-closure discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the rejoin with the planned closure and reduced overtake to about 5 knots by route position, lateral and vertical separation maintained until the closure rate was fully under control. The only refinement available was to hold that same closure control through a faster-than-briefed rejoin. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed rejoin-closure discipline.
texts_above.4: SP managed aspect with small bank adjustments and reduced closure so precisely that route position was reached co-airspeed with Number 1 and no line-of-sight rate, separation never in question at any stage of the rejoin with the transition into fingertip smooth and made only after the aircraft was stabilized in route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional rejoin-closure discipline.
